title: S&P 500 Gets Fresh Warning From 5% Treasury Yield
detail:
S&P 500 Gets Fresh Warning From 5% Treasury Yield
Moz Farooque ACCA
Thu, September 17, 2026 at 12:26 PM MDT 2 min read
^GSPC
QQQ
Trade QQQ on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering just below 5%, putting the S&P 500 near a level that has historically produced some of the market's weakest forward returns.

The benchmark yield eased about seven basis points Thursday morning to roughly 4.95%, after recently moving through a level last seen on a closing basis in 2007.

Is QQQ fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

That 5% threshold matters because history suggests stocks have struggled to generate their usual follow-through when Treasury yields remain that high.

Bespoke Investment Group data show that when the 10-year yield has traded with a 5-handle, the S&P 500 has gained just 0.4% on average over the following three months, with positive returns 56% of the time.

Six-month returns averaged 1.3%, while one-year gains averaged 4.1%.

Those figures compare with much stronger long-term averages of 2.2% over three months, 4.4% over six months and 9.1% over one year.

The historical pattern is not a guarantee of falling stocks.

Higher yields can coexist with equity gains if earnings growth and liquidity remain strong enough to absorb higher borrowing costs. But a 5% Treasury yield reduces the relative attractiveness of stocks because investors can earn more from lower-risk government bonds.

It also compresses the equity risk premium, making stretched valuations harder to justify.

Investors Takeaway

The key question is whether the 10-year yield can remain above 5% rather than simply touching the level.

Thursday's pullback to around 4.95% leaves that question unresolved. A sustained move above 5% would make the weaker historical return pattern more relevant.

For investors, that does not automatically mean selling stocks.

It does mean the hurdle for equities becomes higher. Earnings may need to remain strong enough to offset more attractive bond yields, while richly valued parts of the market could become increasingly sensitive to any disappointment.

History suggests 5% is less a crash signal than a warning that the easy part of the equity rally may be over.

title: If a Bear Market Is Coming, History Says This 1 Investing Decision Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
detail:
If a Bear Market Is Coming, History Says This 1 Investing Decision Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Thu, September 17, 2026 at 12:25 PM MDT 3 min read
^GSPC

Investing in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) via a low-cost exchange-traded fund (ETF), like Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO), is a sound long-term strategy. The benchmark index has generated an average annual total return of about 10% since its inception in 1957, outperforming most individual stocks and actively managed funds over the long term.

But since 1957, there have been ten official bear markets -- peak-to-trough declines of at least 20% -- which occurred every six to seven years. The average bear market only lasts nine to ten months, but those steep downturns drive many investors out of stocks. So if you expect the next bear market to happen in the near future, the best move you can make is to sit still and weather the storm. Let's see why that crucial investing decision could make or break your portfolio.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Why should you resist the urge to sell?

In 1987, the S&P 500 suffered a peak-to-trough decline of 33.5% from August to December -- including the "Black Monday" crash on Oct. 19. From March 2000 to Oct. 2022, the S&P 500 plunged 49.1% as the dot-com bubble burst and the 9/11 attacks derailed the economy.

From Oct. 2007 to March 2009, the Great Recession caused the S&P 500 to sink 56.8%. From Feb. to March 2020, the pandemic caused a 33.9% drop. From Jan. to Oct. 2022, the S&P 500 fell 25.4% as the Fed aggressively hiked its benchmark rates to tame inflation.

But since the beginning of 1987, the S&P 500 has still generated a total return of 6,377%. It's also delivered total returns of 669% and 1,112%, respectively, since the first days of 2007 and 2009. Investors who quit the market too early missed out on those massive gains.

Why should you stay invested?

The S&P 500 is also rebalanced quarterly to include only the 500 largest U.S. companies. By only hosting the winners and pruning the losers, you'll always be exposed to the long-term growth of the U.S. economy. That passive strategy is smarter than rotating your cash to CDs, T-bills, and other fixed-income investments simply because interest rates are rising.

That same logic also applies to individual stocks you're bullish on. Warren Buffett once told investors that if you buy a stock, you should be prepared to "have it go down 50% -- or more -- and be comfortable with it." If you're not, you could leave a lot of money on the table.
